Fixture minute capacity is 30,000 x 2% = 600 shares. Daily capacity is 20,000 x 5% = 1,000 shares. Both conditions must hold, so effective capacity is min(600, 1,000) = 600 shares (scenario-liquidity). The proposed whole order is 1,000 shares: it meets the daily limit exactly but fails the minute limit. The whole order therefore does not pass. Execution is zero under this event's rule; filling 600 shares would impermissibly turn an all-whole-order decision into a partial fill.

The daily pass is meaningful counterevidence to saying all capacity tests fail, but it cannot override the binding minute constraint. Participation limits restrict assumed market impact; volume alone does not demonstrate an executable price, spread, depth, absence of halts or availability of counterparties. The fixture explicitly ignores fees and price limits for this calculation, not for a real trade.

No actual issuer business or sector evidence is supplied. The label ENGINEERING-A is an identifier, not evidence that it belongs to an engineering sector or has a particular business model. The business implication that can be assessed is execution liquidity: a thesis may be attractive yet impossible to implement at the requested size at this decision event. I cannot infer fundamental quality from these synthetic volumes.

Bounded decision: record a failed whole-order capacity gate and retain no invented fill or proceeds. A newly specified smaller order or a later verified executable event would require its own authorized evaluation; neither is supplied here. These authored scenario volumes and ceilings are not market observations and do not amend production policy. Funding, current identity/actions, valuation and other applicable entry conditions remain outside the supplied evidence.
